blocks.text: 1. Semantic Search
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303886-827115318.png
Semantic Search opens the Retrieval module by putting the entire embedding and search pipeline to work, applying everything covered so far to an actual retrieval problem.
It finds chunks whose meaning matches a query, not just its exact wording.
2. ANN Search Algorithms Recap
The ANN Search Algorithms module covered ten topics on how to search vectors quickly, from brute force to DiskANN.
Semantic search puts that entire toolkit to work solving an actual retrieval problem.

blocks.text: 3. Meaning Over Keywords
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447303887-817965371.png
Semantic search converts a query into an embedding and finds the closest stored chunks.
Two differently worded questions with the same intent retrieve the same relevant chunks.
4. The End To End Semantic Search Pipeline

blocks.alt: The End To End Semantic Search Pipeline
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447304096-889547930.png
A query gets embedded using the same model that embedded the stored chunks.
That query vector then gets compared against the stored vectors using the similarity metrics covered earlier.
5. Why Embedding Consistency Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447304097-250636631.png
The query and the stored chunks must come from the same embedding model.
Mismatched models produce vectors in incompatible spaces, making comparison meaningless.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Embedding a query with a different model than the one used for the stored chunks produces meaningless similarity scores, since the two sets of vectors occupy entirely unrelated coordinate spaces.

blocks.text: 6. Approximate Search Under The Hood
A real semantic search system uses an ANN algorithm, not brute force, once collections grow large.
Everything covered across the previous module operates silently underneath every semantic search query.
7. Strengths Of Semantic Search
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447304097-903835090.png
Paraphrases, synonyms, and conceptually related questions all retrieve successfully.
A user asking in their own words still finds the right content.
8. Weaknesses Of Semantic Search Alone
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447304098-440620761.png
A specific product code, error message, or proper noun can get lost among semantically similar but wrong matches.
Semantic search alone is not always enough.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A search for a specific error code can return chunks discussing similar sounding but unrelated errors under semantic search alone, exactly the limitation that keyword search, covered next, addresses.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Semantic Search Is The Right Retrieval Method

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Semantic Search Is The Right Retrieval Method
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447304098-138289893.png
Natural language questions and conceptual queries suit semantic search well.
Exact keyword or code lookup needs keyword search instead, covered as the next topic in this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates a full semantic search pipeline from query embedding through ranked results.

code.content:
chunks = [
    {"id": "c1", "text": "How to reset your account password."},
    {"id": "c2", "text": "Steps for changing your login credentials."},
    {"id": "c3", "text": "Refund policy for damaged products."},
]

def fake_embed(text):
    words = text.lower().split()
    return (
        sum(w in words for w in ["password", "login", "credentials", "reset", "account"]),
        sum(w in words for w in ["refund", "damaged", "product", "policy"]),
    )

def cosine_like_similarity(v1, v2):
    dot = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(v1, v2))
    mag1 = sum(a * a for a in v1) ** 0.5
    mag2 = sum(a * a for a in v2) ** 0.5
    return dot / (mag1 * mag2) if mag1 and mag2 else 0

chunk_embeddings = {c["id"]: fake_embed(c["text"]) for c in chunks}
query = "I forgot my login and need to change it"
query_embedding = fake_embed(query)

print(f"Query: {query!r}\n")
results = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: -cosine_like_similarity(query_embedding, chunk_embeddings[c["id"]]))
for c in results:
    score = cosine_like_similarity(query_embedding, chunk_embeddings[c["id"]])
    print(f"  {c['id']}: {score:.2f} - {c['text']}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the query matching the password related chunks most strongly despite sharing no exact words like "password" with the query text.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Embedding a query with a different model than the one used to embed the stored chunks.
Using semantic search alone for queries that require exact keyword or code precision.
Forgetting that a real semantic search system relies on an ANN algorithm, not brute force, at scale.
Assuming semantic search always outperforms exact matching regardless of the query type.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Semantic search finds chunks whose meaning matches a query, not just its exact wording.
It puts the entire embedding and ANN search toolkit covered so far to practical use.
A query gets embedded using the same model that embedded the stored chunks, then compared.
The query and stored chunks must share the same embedding model to produce meaningful comparisons.
A real system relies on an ANN algorithm underneath, not brute force, once collections grow large.
Paraphrases, synonyms, and conceptually related questions all retrieve successfully.
Specific codes, error messages, or proper nouns can get lost among semantically similar matches.
Semantic search alone is not always sufficient for every kind of query.
Next up: Keyword Search, covering the exact term matching approach that complements semantic search.
